analysis.one_liner: Requires voters to give an excuse and apply early to get a federal absentee ballot.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, was referred to committee the day it was introduced, and died there without ever coming up for a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal election law so that no state could mail an absentee ballot to a voter in a federal election unless the voter applied by noon on the Friday before Election Day, stated an approved reason for not voting in person (such as work, caregiving, disability, or being out of town), and included a sworn statement of identity. It would end no-excuse mail voting in every state for federal elections. The bill was introduced by one House Republican, attracted no cosponsors, and was sent to committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The record names no beneficiary group. The practical effect would fall on incumbent federal officeholders, who face fewer ballots to contest when voters must meet a strict deadline, state a specific excuse, and have each application reviewed before receiving a ballot. Voters whose work schedules, caregiving duties, disabilities, or travel keep them from the polls on Election Day would lose the option of simply requesting a mail ballot.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's stated purpose, in its text and title, is to set uniform requirements for absentee voting in federal elections, on the theory that requiring a specific excuse and an early, sworn application makes the process more uniform and accountable.

It would apply one national deadline — an application received by noon on the Friday before the election — and one national list of qualifying reasons (work, constant caregiving, physical ailment or disability, absence from the jurisdiction, or another federal law) to every state's federal elections.

analysis.who_pays: Voters who cannot easily reach a polling place: people whose jobs block them on Election Day, caregivers of a parent, spouse, or child needing constant care, voters with disabilities or physical ailments, and anyone out of town. Each would have to file a written application with a stated excuse and sworn identity statement by noon on the Friday before the election, and state and local election offices would have to review and adjudicate every application and excuse.
analysis.who_pays_short: Shift workers, caregivers, and disabled voters

drawbacks.text: The bill would end no-excuse mail voting nationwide for federal elections. In states that currently let any voter request an absentee ballot, every one of those voters would instead need to state a qualifying reason and file by noon on the Friday before Election Day or be refused a ballot.

The bill adds paperwork and deadlines precisely for the voters least able to absorb them — workers with rigid shifts, people providing constant care, and voters with disabilities — and requires election officials to judge whether each stated reason qualifies, creating grounds for applications to be denied.

The bill text contains no findings that existing absentee procedures have produced fraud or problems, so the costs to voters are imposed without the record showing what problem the restrictions would solve.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are concrete and borne by identifiable voters, while the benefit is limited to the general argument for stricter uniform rules. Any voter who misses the Friday-noon application deadline, or whose stated reason an official judges insufficient, simply does not get a federal ballot. The bill offers no new protections, funding, or process improvements to offset that burden.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Glenn Grothman introduced the bill on May 22, 2024, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor, from either party.
The committee took no further action, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill never reported out or brought to the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary voters who rely on absentee ballots are better off, because the restrictions never became law. Incumbent officeholders lost a proposal that would have made ballots marginally easier to limit.

for.name: Rep. Glenn Grothman
for.role: Sponsor; introduced the bill and referred it to committee

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only sponsor was a Republican, and no member of either party cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would add a deadline, a required excuse, and a sworn statement to every federal absentee ballot request, so fewer applications would be approved and fewer ballots counted. Candidates running for re-election benefit when fewer voters participate, which is why voting-access groups generally treat such restrictions as favoring incumbents.

Officials in states with no-excuse mail voting would have to reverse procedures and instead review the excuse on every federal absentee application by a new mid-week deadline, adding work and rejection decisions. The bill provides no funding for the added burden.
